content.title: About
content.content: Beignet is a traditional French fried dough pastry, often dusted with powdered sugar. The batter is usually made from flour, eggs, milk, butter and yeast, then small portions are deep‑fried until golden. The taste is mildly sweet with a crisp outer crust and a soft, airy interior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beignets are especially popular in New Orleans, where they are commonly served with powdered sugar and coffee.
The classic recipe uses a yeasted dough, but there are quick‑rise versions that rely on baking powder.
In France, beignets are sold as round “pancake‑like” treats from street stalls.
They became famous in the U.S. through the Café du Monde brand in the late 19th century.
Both sweet and savory versions exist; savory beignets may contain cheese, ham or seafood.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Beignets provide carbohydrates that quickly supply the body with energy.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs and milk in the batter add a modest amount of animal protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeasted dough is a source of B1, B2 and B6 vitamins, important for metabolism.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Flour and yeast contribute a small amount of iron, supporting blood health.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: Milk and butter add calcium, beneficial for bone strength.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Because they are deep‑fried, beignets are high in calories and saturated fats.

items.title: Sugar
items.content: They are often dusted with powdered sugar, increasing simple sugar intake.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The batter is typically made with wheat flour, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Trans fats from reused oil
items.content: Reusing frying oil can create trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve beignets hot, dusted with powdered sugar, with honey, fruit sauce, or plain. They can be split and filled with sweet cream, jam, or savory fillings such as cheese and ham.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Beignets are best enjoyed fresh and hot. If needed, keep them in an airtight container at room temperature for 1‑2 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a bag and reheat in the oven before serving.

brussels-sprouts-frozen-cooked-no-added-.title: Brussels sprouts, frozen, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brussels sprouts are small cabbage-like heads harvested as compact buds. This product is frozen, pre‑cooked sprouts with no added fat. Rapid freezing after harvest locks in nutrients and flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The vegetable is named after Brussels, where it was first cultivated in the 16th century.
One serving (100 g) provides about 43 kcal, making it a low‑calorie food.
Sprouts are rich in glucoraphanin, a compound that supports gut health.
Freezing preserves the bright green color and a crisp texture after reheating.
Brussels sprouts belong to the cruciferous family, along with broccoli and cauliflower.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and acts as a powerful antioxidant.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate supports DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: No added fat makes this product suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Cruciferous allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to cabbage family vegetables.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Compounds in sprouts can cause bloating or gas in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Glucoraphanin content
items.content: Large amounts may cause gastrointestinal discomfort for some people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the frozen sprouts by steaming, microwaving, or sautéing without oil. They can be added to salads, soups, stews, or served as a side dish with meat or fish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C or lower. After thawing, consume within 1–2 days and do not re‑freeze; refrigerated leftovers should be used within 24 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Garlic (Allium sativum) is a bulb vegetable native to Central Asia and a close relative of onions, leeks, and chives. Each bulb is made up of several cloves wrapped in papery skin. It has a pungent, savory aroma and flavor that mellows and sweetens when cooked. Garlic is used worldwide as a flavoring and has a long history in traditional medicine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Garlic has been cultivated for more than 5,000 years.
When garlic is crushed or chopped, an enzyme reaction forms allicin, which gives it its sharp smell.
Letting chopped garlic rest for about ten minutes before cooking can help preserve its beneficial compounds.
Black garlic is whole garlic aged under controlled heat and humidity, giving it a sweet, soft texture.
Garlic is one of the most widely used seasonings in the world.

items.title: Contains sulfur compounds
items.content: Allicin and other organosulfur compounds in garlic are being studied for their biological activity.

items.title: Provides manganese and vitamin B6
items.content: These nutrients support normal metabolism.

items.title: Provides vitamin C and selenium
items.content: These support immune function and antioxidant defenses, though garlic is usually eaten in small amounts.

items.title: May support heart health
items.content: Some studies suggest that garlic may help improve certain cardiovascular markers, although more research is needed.

items.title: Adds flavor without salt
items.content: Garlic can add taste to food and reduce the need for added salt.

items.title: Breath and body odor
items.content: Garlic can cause strong breath and body odor.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Garlic may cause heartburn, gas, or stomach upset in some people, especially raw.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: Large amounts or garlic supplements may affect blood clotting and interact with some medications. People taking blood thinners or planning surgery should consult a healthcare professional.

items.title: Garlic in oil
items.content: Garlic stored in oil at room temperature can grow the bacteria that cause botulism. Refrigerate garlic-in-oil mixtures and use them quickly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Garlic can be minced, sliced, crushed, roasted whole, sautéed, or added to sauces, soups, marinades, dressings, and spreads. Raw garlic has the strongest flavor, while roasted garlic is mild and sweet. Add it near the end of sautéing so it does not burn and turn bitter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store whole garlic bulbs in a cool, dry, dark, well-ventilated place, where they keep for weeks to months. Do not refrigerate whole bulbs for long, as this can cause sprouting. Peeled or chopped garlic should be refrigerated in an airtight container and used within a few days. Do not keep garlic in oil at room temperature.

content.title: About
content.content: Grape juice drink, light is a non‑alcoholic beverage made from 100 % grape juice diluted with water and lightly sweetened. It offers a bright fruity flavor, low calorie count, and a gentle carbonation, making it popular among both children and adults looking for a refreshing and healthier option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Grape juice contains polyphenols such as resveratrol, known for antioxidant properties.
The light version typically contains about 5 g of sugar per 100 ml, roughly half of regular fruit juices.
Grape varieties used are often sourced from temperate regions where berries have high sugar and aromatic compound levels.
The drink can be still or lightly carbonated, influencing taste perception.
Many light grape juice drinks are fortified with vitamin C to boost immune support.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Polyphenols and flavonoids in grape juice help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Resveratrol may improve endothelial function and lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: High water content aids in maintaining proper fluid balance.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Fortified vitamin C enhances immune function and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: The light formulation provides fewer calories, useful for weight management.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Even reduced, the drink still contains sugar that can affect blood glucose levels.

items.title: Grape allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to grape components.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic pH may irritate sensitive tooth enamel; rinsing the mouth after consumption is advisable.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some versions may include preservatives (e.g., potassium sorbate) which can be problematic for sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the drink chilled on its own, add it to smoothies, cocktails, or use as a base for fruit punches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep refrigerated and consume within 5‑7 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Frozen cheese pizza with a thick crust is a ready‑to‑bake product made from dough, tomato sauce, cheese, and sometimes additional toppings. The dough is denser, giving a crispy yet tender crust after baking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first mass‑produced frozen pizza is often credited to Totino's in the 1960s in the USA.
A thick crust requires a longer bake time, typically 12‑15 minutes at 200 °C (400 °F).
Cheese blends usually combine mozzarella and cheddar for optimal melt and flavor.
Frozen pizzas can be stored up to 12 months at a constant –18 °C (0 °F).
In Russia popular brands include Semeyny, Burger King, and Papa John’s offering thick‑crust options.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: The cheese provides calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: The dough supplies carbohydrates for quick energy.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Cheese and optional meat toppings deliver protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Dough and cheese contain B1, B2, and B6 vitamins that support metabolism.

items.title: Convenient meal option
items.content: Fast preparation makes it a handy choice for busy schedules, adding variety to the diet.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheese and sauce can be salty, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Thick crust and cheese increase calorie count; portion control is advised.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Some pre‑made doughs may contain partially hydrogenated oils.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Contains dairy and gluten, which can trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Ingredient quality
items.content: Lower‑quality additives can reduce the nutritional value of the product.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Preheat the oven to 200 °C (400 °F). Place the pizza on a rack or baking sheet and bake for 12‑15 minutes until the crust is golden and the cheese is melted. Let stand 2‑3 minutes before slicing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen pizza in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once thawed, use within 24 hours and do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Strawberries are edible berries of the plant Fragaria × ananassa, cultivated in temperate regions. The fruits are bright red, sweet‑tart, and juicy. Strawberries are eaten fresh, used in desserts, baked goods, smoothies, and jams.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Strawberries are one of the few berry plants whose seeds are also edible.
They contain more vitamin C than oranges by about 30 %.
There are over 600 strawberry varieties differing in size, aroma, and harvest time.
Strawberries are a symbol of spring and feature in many cultural celebrations.
The first cultivated strawberries appeared in Europe in the 18th century.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that supports immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids such as anthocyanins help combat free radicals and reduce chronic disease risk.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Strawberries provide potassium and dietary fiber, which help maintain normal blood pressure and cholesterol levels.

items.title: Aids blood sugar control
items.content: Low glycemic index and fiber slow sugar absorption.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and especially beneficial for pregnant women.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to strawberries, such as skin itching or swelling.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Strawberries are often treated with pesticides; thorough washing or choosing organic berries is recommended.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Strawberries can be eaten fresh, added to yogurt, cereals, salads, desserts, and smoothies. They can also be made into jam, sauce, or frozen for later use.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store strawberries in the refrigerator in their original container or a shallow bowl covered with plastic wrap. Use within 2–3 days. Do not wash until ready to eat to prevent spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Yogurt is a fermented dairy product made by inoculating milk with specific bacterial cultures. This version uses whole cow’s milk (NS) and is flavored with non‑fruit options such as vanilla, caramel, nut, or spice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Yogurt originated in Central Asia more than 5,000 years ago.
Traditional preparation involved fermenting milk in clay pots at room temperature.
Different countries have their own styles: Greek yogurt is thick, Turkish yogurt is more liquid, and Scandinavian varieties are often fortified with vitamins D and B12.
Yogurt can be pasteurized or raw; raw versions contain more live cultures but require strict quality control.
Non‑fruit flavors are usually derived from natural extracts, spices, and plant essences.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Yogurt provides live cultures of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium that support gut microbiota.

items.title: Calcium and Vitamin D
items.content: The dairy base supplies high levels of calcium, and added vitamin D enhances its absorption.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Yogurt is a good source of complete protein, aiding tissue repair and satiety.

items.title: Reduced Lactose
items.content: Fermentation breaks down part of the lactose, making yogurt easier to digest for those with mild lactose intolerance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yogurt contains vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may react to yogurt.

items.title: Added sugar in flavored versions
items.content: Some non‑fruit flavorings contain added sugars, increasing calorie content.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: After opening, live cultures diminish quickly, so consume within a few days.

items.title: Probiotic imbalance
items.content: Excessive consumption can cause temporary gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Yogurt can be enjoyed on its own, mixed into oatmeal, smoothies, or used as a base for sauces and desserts. Non‑fruit varieties pair well with honey, nuts, granola, or spices such as cinnamon and cardamom.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep yogurt refrigerated at 2‑4 °C in its original container. After opening, seal tightly and consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if it develops off‑odors or an unusual texture.
